nameStory: The Brown Roll-Rim gets its memorable name from its distinctive cap edge, which stays tightly curled inward like a cinnamon roll throughout its life. This "rolled rim" is so characteristic that you can spot it from across the forest floor. The brown part is obvious - these mushrooms come in various shades of brown, from coffee to chocolate.
description: The Brown Roll-Rim is a medium-sized mushroom with a funnel-shaped brown cap and an unmistakable tightly inrolled edge. Despite having gills like typical mushrooms, it's actually more closely related to pored mushrooms like boletes - a fascinating example of how looks can be deceiving in the fungus world! The cap grows up to about 5 inches across, while the whole mushroom reaches up to 2-3 inches tall. You'll notice the gills run down the stem and may look almost pore-like near the base.

idTips.label: Cap Edge
idTips.description: The rim stays tightly rolled inward like a scroll throughout the mushroom's life - this is the signature feature that makes identification easy

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Funnel-shaped and various shades of brown, from light tan to dark chocolate, with a smooth or slightly sticky surface when moist

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Run down the stem (decurrent) and may look pore-like near the stem base, yellowish-brown and easily bruised darker when handled

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Short and stout, same brown color as cap or slightly paler, solid and firm to the touch

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Gills and flesh bruise darker brown when pressed or cut, reaction happens within minutes

idTips.label: Safety Warning
idTips.description: DEADLY POISONOUS - Never eat this mushroom! Can cause fatal autoimmune reactions even in people who have eaten it safely before

habitat: Look for Brown Roll-Rims in both deciduous and coniferous forests throughout New England, especially under birch, pine, and oak trees. They form beneficial partnerships with tree roots (mycorrhizal relationships), so you'll find them in healthy forest soil rather than on decaying wood. They also pop up in grassy areas near woodlands and can be quite common in mixed forests with rich, moist soil.

seasonality.spring: Not typically found in spring - the fungal network is underground preparing for later fruiting.
seasonality.summer: May begin appearing in late summer during warm, moist periods after good rains.
seasonality.fall: Peak season! Most abundant from late August through October when temperatures cool and autumn rains arrive.
seasonality.winter: Disappears with hard frosts, though the underground fungal network remains alive and connected to tree roots.

funFact: This innocent-looking mushroom was responsible for the death of a respected German mushroom expert in 1944, leading scientists to discover it can trigger your immune system to attack your own red blood cells - even if you've eaten it safely for years without problems!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with edible oyster mushrooms or other brown gilled fungi, but the tightly inrolled rim that never flattens out is unique to roll-rims. Memory trick: "If the rim won't unroll, don't eat at all!" The rolled edge stays tight throughout the mushroom's entire life, unlike most mushrooms whose caps flatten with age.
contextualKnowledge: Despite having gills like typical mushrooms, genetic testing shows Brown Roll-Rims are actually more closely related to pored boletes - a reminder that mushroom relationships aren't always what they appear to be! This species was considered edible in parts of Europe for centuries before its deadly nature was discovered.
compareHints: Brown Roll-Rim is the most common roll-rim species in New England, distinguished from its relative the Coppery Pax by its consistently brown coloration and woodland habitat. While Coppery Pax has more reddish or copper tones and prefers wetter areas, Brown Roll-Rim sticks to its various shades of brown and typical forest settings. Both share that characteristic inrolled rim, but the Brown Roll-Rim is much more frequently encountered.
